connector: Chapter 5 ended with Master’s death and everyone in the quarters afraid of being sold. Harriet told John she was going to run away. He grabbed her wrist and said she would never make it. She walked out without a word. In Chapter 6, follow each step she takes, in order, and ask what it takes to leave for a North she has never seen.

a.raw: first harriet visited the quaker lady then she told her brothers finally she sang a goodbye song
a.fixed: First, Harriet visited the Quaker lady. Then she told her brothers. Finally, she sang a goodbye song.
a.why: Capital F on First, with a comma after the time word; capital H on Harriet (a name); capital Q on Quaker (the name of a church group); a period after ‘lady’ and after ‘brothers’; capital T on Then; capital F on Finally, with a comma after it.

b.fixed: First, Harriet packed her ticking bag. Then she left her quilt for the Quaker lady. Finally, she sang a farewell song.
b.why: Capital F on First, with a comma after the time word; capital H on Harriet; a period after ‘bag’; capital T on Then; capital Q on Quaker (a church group’s name); a period after ‘lady’; capital F on Finally, with a comma after it.

fill1.h1: This machine lets you hear a voice from a faraway place. Which part means far?
fill1.why: tele- means far: tele + phone = a voice or sound carried from far away.

fill2.h1: This screen shows pictures that were sent from far away. Which part means far?
fill2.why: tele- means far: tele + vision = seeing pictures from far away.

fill3.h1: A car seems to move all on its own, with no horse to pull it. Which part means self?
fill3.why: auto- means self: auto + mobile = something that moves by itself.

fill4.h1: A door that opens with nobody pushing it works this way. Which part means self?
fill4.why: auto- means self: auto + matic = working by itself.

notes.wgrd: In a biography, big moments have a before and an after. Find the turning point, retell the steps that come next in order with time words, and ask how each step caused the next one.
vocab: The order in which events happened, from first to last.
A personal account of what someone has seen or done.
The act of being set free.
notes.wordParts: tele- means “far” or “far away,” and auto- means “self.” A telescope helps you see something far away. An autograph is your own name, written by you: telephone, television, automobile, autobiography.
notes.grammar: A comparative adjective compares two things. It often ends in -er or uses more: darker, more afraid. A superlative compares three or more and often ends in -est or uses most: the bravest of the four.
notes.spelling: Some verbs keep their spelling when -ion is added: act becomes action. Others change first. In decide, the final de turns into s: decision. In permit, the t turns into ss: permission.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. Chapter 5 ended with Master’s death, and with Harriet saying it out loud to John, one slow word at a time: I’m going to run away. He told her she’d never make it. In my research notes, Chapter 6 gets a whole page of its own. Today’s question: what does it take to step off the plantation, alone, toward a North you’ve never seen?
transcripts.guide2: Freedom Watch: the moment of decision. On my tours, people asked me when Harriet made up her mind. I used to say it was one big moment. Now that I’ve read more, I’m not so sure. In this chapter, watch for every time she has a reason to stop, and what she does instead. The road she knows isn’t safe. The road north is a mystery. Which is scarier?
transcripts.read: Before you open Chapter 6, get your sequence notes ready. This chapter moves fast, and the order matters. Watch the Quaker lady, and how carefully Harriet speaks to her. Listen for the words thee and thy; that’s how Quakers talked. Keep an eye on what Harriet carries, and on one thing she gives away. Listen for a song, too. Sterling prints every word of it.

wordgame.voice: Tap a word part, then the word it finishes. Or drag the part onto the word. Ask what each word is about: something far away, or something that works by itself?

why.t: In Chapter 5, Harriet sews her own patchwork quilt, as warm and beautiful as her mother’s, and pulls it around her shoulders to look for the North Star through the cracks in the roof. In Chapter 6, she lays it on the Quaker lady’s doorstep: thank you and farewell. tele- means far, and auto- means self. Each right word sews one patch into the quilt. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: The quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. tele- = far, auto- = self.

songs.title: Bound for the Promised Land
lines: I’m bound for the promised land.
Friends, I’m going to leave you.
I’m sorry, friends, to leave you.
But I’ll meet you in the morning.
I’ll meet you in the morning
When you reach the promised land;
On the other side of the Jordan,
For I’m bound for the promised land.
songs.heard: A church song about dying and going to heaven, the promised land on the other side of the Jordan River. Anyone passing the quarters would hear a hymn.
songs.meant: Goodbye. Harriet was leaving for the free North, on her own, and she would see them again someday. Her family would know the traders had not taken her.
songs.q: Miss Sarah’s brother has just ridden by and glared at Harriet and Mary Ann. Why does Harriet sing her goodbye instead of saying it?
songs.a: Saying “I’m running away” out loud could get her caught. A church song was safe to sing, and the people who loved her would understand it.

ft.songsIntro: In Chapter 6, Harriet has to let her family know she is leaving, so they won’t think the slave traders took her. But it isn’t safe to visit their cabin, and someone is watching. So she sings.

catcher.title: Before, turn, after
